articles.title: EU Moves to Strengthen Eastern Border Infrastructure
articles.summaryB1: The European Union is planning to spend more money on roads and railways near its eastern borders. This will help countries like Poland, Lithuania and Romania to connect better with the rest of Europe. EU leaders agreed that better transport links are important for the economy and for security. The money will come from a special EU fund. Work on the new infrastructure is expected to start next year. Many people who live near the border are happy about this decision. They hope that better roads will also bring more jobs to their region. Poland will receive one of the largest shares of the funding because it has the longest eastern border in the EU. Local governments are already making plans for how to use the money.

vocabularyB1.definition: The basic systems a country needs, like roads, railways and power supplies

articles.summaryB2: The European Commission has unveiled a comprehensive package to bolster transport and logistical infrastructure along the EU's eastern flank, with particular emphasis on Poland, the Baltic states and Romania. The initiative draws on the Cohesion Fund and newly established defence-linked financing instruments, aiming to dual-purpose civilian infrastructure for potential military mobility requirements — a concept increasingly central to NATO's strategic posture in the region. Poland stands to receive a disproportionately large allocation given the extent of its eastern border. Critics have raised questions about procurement timelines and the adequacy of environmental impact assessments, while some MEPs have called for greater transparency in the tendering process. Proponents argue that the security and economic rationale is compelling, particularly given recent geopolitical tensions.

vocabularyB2.definition: To strengthen or improve something significantly

articles.title: Tech Giants Face New EU Digital Rules This Autumn
articles.summaryB1: Big technology companies like Google and Meta will have to follow new rules in Europe from this autumn. The rules are part of a plan to make the internet safer and more fair for everyone. Companies that break the rules can be fined a lot of money — up to ten percent of their total income. European countries, including Poland, supported these new regulations strongly. Users will have more control over their personal information and how it is used. The new rules also mean that large companies cannot stop smaller companies from competing with them. Poland's digital ministry has been one of the most active supporters of strict enforcement. Many Polish internet users say they feel better protected because of these changes.

vocabularyB1.definition: Official rules made by a government or authority
Making sure that rules are followed

Trying to be more successful than others in the same market
Kept safe from harm or unfair treatment

articles.summaryB2: The Digital Markets Act enforcement timeline has been accelerated, with the European Commission confirming that designated 'gatekeepers' — including Alphabet, Meta and Apple — must demonstrate full compliance by October. The regulation targets anti-competitive behaviour, mandatory interoperability between platforms, and greater algorithmic transparency. Poland's digital ministry has been notably vocal in pushing for stricter enforcement mechanisms, reflecting broader Central European frustration with the perceived dominance of American platforms in local media ecosystems. Non-compliance carries penalties of up to 10% of global annual turnover, with repeat offenders facing structural remedies including forced divestiture. Legal analysts expect several major platforms to challenge the rules in the Court of Justice of the EU.

articles.title: Central European Cities Tackle Summer Heat With Green Spaces
articles.summaryB1: Cities in Central Europe, including Warsaw and Prague, are planting more trees and building new parks to deal with very hot summers. Scientists say that cities are getting hotter because of climate change. Green spaces help to cool the air and make life more comfortable for people. Local governments are spending large amounts of money on these projects. Residents say they are very happy about the changes. In Warsaw, the city plans to plant thousands of new trees along busy streets over the next three years. Prague is also creating several new parks in areas where there were previously only buildings. Both cities say that these green areas are not just nice to look at — they are necessary for people's health and well-being during extreme heat.

vocabularyB1.definition: Long-term changes in global temperatures and weather patterns, mainly caused by humans
People who live in a particular place
Temperatures that are much higher than normal and potentially dangerous

At an earlier time; before something else happened

articles.summaryB2: Municipal authorities across Central Europe are implementing 'sponge city' strategies as urban heat islands intensify under accelerating climate projections. Warsaw's latest masterplan earmarks 18% of all new development land for permeable surfaces and expanding tree canopy, while Kraków has introduced mandatory heat-resilience requirements into its building codes. Urban planners acknowledge a fundamental tension between densification pressures — driven by acute housing shortages — and the imperative to preserve green corridors that regulate urban microclimates. Research from the Warsaw University of Life Sciences suggests that mature street trees can reduce local temperatures by up to 8°C on peak summer days, lending scientific weight to what critics had previously dismissed as a purely aesthetic concern.
